text: A written plan prevents this by closing decisions in advance. … when it lives in a file, replacing it is a visible AMENDMENT with a written reason.
`workspace/plan.md` is the one memory that survives — if it exists when you start, READ IT FIRST and continue it; never write a competing second plan.
note: Site: plan.md is "your plan and your memory" (A1).

text: The more famous the client, the more your memory volunteers content the brief never asked for — products, events, dates, speakers.
The plan is a WORKING ARTIFACT, never an approval gate. You write it and proceed — you do not stop to ask permission unless the user asked for plan-only work.
Substantial builds: a fresh page, a campaign page, a multi-section brief, a whole-page rebuild. Not for small scoped edits

1. Anchors — attributed user requirements, working choices and evidence 2. Grammar audit — the measured visual law of this client's site 3. Sections — one spec per band, each with a named source 4. Review & finish — the acceptance walk, written before building
note: Site: message plan, then each section with its clone and words (A1, D1).

text: User requirement … Working choice … Evidence … A delegation brief is an agent-authored summary. Extract useful context without turning its emphatic wording into a user quote.
note: Site A1 treats the brief's goal, reader and offer as fixed.

text: A simple request for an account page does not specify a pilot, navigation logos, a demo offer or a number of sections. Choose any missing audience detail, offer/action and shell deliberately, with a short reason; keep those choices revisable.
Hero archetype (split? centered? what carries the visual weight?) · Section rhythm … · Image-to-copy ratio … · The recognizability test

Question: the one visitor question this band answers … Adds: what the reader learns here beyond the preceding bands · Words: actual heading, explanation and card/panel copy … Evidence: … Actions: each retained button's label, destination/behavior and purpose
A section with no named source, or answering no question, does not go in the plan.

A second product exhibit earns space by answering a different question, not because the library has another attractive screenshot. Merge repeated arguments while preserving useful explanation; do not solve length by making type smaller.
Write the acceptance walk BEFORE building, so review criteria cannot be invented afterward to match whatever got built
Each section entry carries `[status: planned | built | verified]`. Update it as you go
Update the active section record in plan.md FIRST, retain a short change note, then act on it. `AMENDMENT: <what changes> — <why> — <which sections it affects>`
note: Site A1: "If you change your mind, update plan.md first."

text: An inferred offer can change for a documented reason; an explicit user offer cannot silently become a different one.
Your finalize report states plan-vs-built: which sections shipped as planned, every amendment with its reason, and the final status of every section.
